title: 90,000 London Professional Jobs Forecast to Move to UK Regions by 2031
excerpt: Analysis by Robert Walters projects a £9 billion boost to regional economies as bankers, lawyers and accountants leave the capital amid rising costs and devolution push
body:
• Up to 90,000 bankers, lawyers and accountants could see their roles relocated from London to regional UK cities by 2031, according to recruitment firm Robert Walters
  • The shift is expected to inject £9 billion into regional economies, rising to £15 billion when factoring in local spending and supply chain effects
  • Manchester and the northwest are the biggest beneficiaries, forecast to gain 22,500 jobs worth £2.25 billion by 2031
  • The trend aligns with Prime Minister Andy Burnham's devolution drive to deliver "good growth in every postcode"

As many as 90,000 white-collar professionals based in London are forecast to have their jobs moved to regional cities across the UK over the next five years, according to a new analysis by Robert Walters, the listed recruitment company.

The projected migration of bankers, lawyers and accountants represents 2.5 per cent of London's overall workforce and is estimated to bring a £9 billion boost to regional economies including Leeds, Manchester and Birmingham. That figure could rise to £15 billion when accounting for the transplants' spending in their new home towns and the extra work it would generate for local supply chains.

What's Driving the Exodus

Robert Walters said more companies were looking to move teams out of London because of spiralling costs. A shortage of "prime" office space has pushed London office rents to record highs, making regional alternatives increasingly attractive.

"Our forecast indicates a rebalancing of the scales towards stronger regional jobs growth over a widespread shift of business activity away from London."

— Jonny Bohane, Robert Walters market intelligence team

The analysis used past job relocations from major UK employers to establish a baseline, then combined Robert Walters' own placement volumes with LinkedIn movement data to project regional hiring demand. The model also factored in office capacity, hybrid working levels, the depth of local talent pools, regional development initiatives and government decentralisation programmes.

Regional Winners

The northwest of England, including Manchester and Liverpool, is forecast to be the biggest beneficiary, attracting 22,500 jobs by 2031 and injecting up to £2.25 billion into the region's economy. Manchester's status as the UK's second hub for growth continues to solidify — Siemens moved its UK headquarters there from Surrey in 2019, and the city already hosts major offices for professional services firms.

About a fifth of all relocated positions — up to 18,000 — could end up in the Midlands, principally Birmingham, bringing a £1.8 billion economic boost. Birmingham is home to the second-largest UK office of Deloitte, the Big Four accounting firm.

Yorkshire stands to attract about 13,500 London leavers, adding £1.35 billion to the local economy. The Bank of England has pledged to have one in ten of its workforce based out of Leeds from 2027.

The remaining 36,000 or so jobs are set to relocate to other major regional cities including Bristol, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Cambridge, Newcastle, Liverpool, Reading and Cardiff.

Burnham's Devolution Agenda

The forecast relocations align with the devolution ambitions of Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has promised to reduce the country's reliance on London, which accounts for about a quarter of the UK's economic output. Last month, Burnham opened a northern branch of Downing Street, No 10 North, as part of his broader push for regional growth.

By end of 2027, Robert Walters predicts up to 12,000 jobs will have already moved out of the capital, with the outflow expected to reach 45,000 by 2029. Senior leadership teams are likely to remain in London, with companies bolstering junior ranks with local talent in regional offices.

What It Means for Indian Professionals in the UK

For the thousands of Indian-origin professionals working in London's financial and legal sectors, the trend could present both opportunities and disruption. Those willing to relocate to regional hubs like Manchester, Birmingham or Leeds could benefit from lower living costs while maintaining career trajectories at major firms. However, the shift may also reshape immigration patterns and visa sponsorship strategies for companies increasingly anchored outside the capital.

Daniel Harris, UK managing director at Robert Walters, said the trend would accelerate as "cost considerations remain high, and hybrid working allows organisations to build more geographically diverse teams."
nri_angle: Thousands of Indian-origin professionals work in London's financial and legal sectors. This shift could reshape career opportunities, living costs, and visa sponsorship patterns for the UK's Indian community.
